title: The mid-project curveball
intro: Phase 1 just merged. Then marketing calls: 'it has to work on phones for the conference booth.' Steer the project — and watch the sync meter.

nodes.text: A real product change (responsive design) has arrived mid-project. It's not on the roadmap and no spec mentions it. What do you do?

choices.label: Hand-edit the CSS yourself — it's just a few media queries
choices.note: You patched code the specs know nothing about.

choices.label: Pause on a replanning branch and assess the change with the agent
choices.note: You made the pause a normal, deliberate step.

nodes.text: The booth demo works… but requirements.md still says nothing about responsiveness, and the agent's next feature ships a fixed-width page. Reviews get slower; someone starts a private notes file. This is drift. Recover?

choices.label: Run a replanning pass to resync specs, code, and roadmap
choices.note: Recovered — later and more expensively than a pause would have cost.

nodes.text: On the replanning branch the agent sizes the change: viewport meta, mobile-first CSS, one new test. Small, and early in the project. How do you land it?

choices.label: Implement it now, updating product specs + feature specs + code together
choices.note: Right call for small-and-early: everything moves in one pass.

choices.label: Schedule it as its own roadmap phase regardless of size
choices.note: Defensible — but for a change this small you paid process overhead for no extra safety.

nodes.text: While you're paused, you notice you've typed the same 'update the changelog before merging' prompt four times this month. Do you do anything about it?

choices.label: Package it as a skill and invoke /changelog from now on
choices.note: Replanning improved the WORKFLOW, not just the project.

choices.label: Keep retyping it — writing a skill feels like yak-shaving
choices.note: The repeated prompt keeps taxing every future feature.

ending.principle: Run slow to run fast: replanning is a normal step that makes the next feature cheaper than the last.
ending.debrief: You absorbed a product change without drift (specs, code, and roadmap moved together), sized it honestly (small + early → do it now; big → its own phase), and turned a repeated prompt into a skill. That's all three radii of replanning: the feature, the project, the workflow.

ending.principle: Replanning that only fixes the project — and not the workflow — leaves speed on the table.
ending.debrief: The specs and code are back in sync, which is the important half. But the prompts you retype are process debt: the moment you catch yourself repeating one, that's the signal to package it as a skill.
